source.title: Towards Generating Informative Textual Description for Neurons in Language Models
source.authors: Shrayani Mondal; Rishabh Garodia; Arbaaz Qureshi; Taesung Lee; Youngja Park

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a method for assigning textual descriptors to neurons, but does not test any of the listed claim versions: it does not estimate the share of neurons with one or more jobs, test out-of-sample firing predictions, or evaluate the other stated claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron-descriptor precision, recall, and consistency, recorded below as results about neuron descriptions that do not test a listed version. Its sentence-label annotation results and cited findings are not neuron-level results bearing on a version.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a method that assigns textual descriptors to BERT-base [CLS] neurons from top-1% activating Amazon reviews. It reports only how well the method performs: precision@2, recall@2 and Jaccard consistency on 10 neurons. It does not estimate the share of neurons with one main job, test the InceptionV1 example, vary architecture or tools to track interpretable shares, build attribution graphs, or score explanations by predicting activations on new text. Its consistency check re-derives descriptors on a disjoint split rather than predicting firing, so it does not test V6 or V7. Some would call this T4, since it reports its own method's performance, but it does not rely on the claim's finding, so T6/discusses stands.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude their unsupervised framework explains neurons with human-interpretable descriptors at reasonable precision and recall, and that it scales to other datasets and text models.
record.recipe_differences: The study generates dataset-specific descriptors using generative language models and clustering, then assigns them to BERT neurons from highly activating review examples. It does not perform the pole audit described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Descriptor consistency changes with composition threshold: the average neuron-level Jaccard similarity peaks at 0.35 and drops beyond that; the paper also reports that descriptor-level similarity peaks at 0.45 and drops sharply at 0.5.

fits_no_version.finding: On 10 random BERT-base [CLS] neurons, LLM-generated descriptors assigned from top-1% activating reviews reached precision@2 75% and recall@2 50% against ChatGPT labels. Descriptor sets from disjoint data halves had Jaccard similarity 0.95 at threshold 0.35.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised descriptor assignment from activating examples gives moderately precise, split-stable neuron descriptions in BERT on review data.

record.code_released: not stated; the authors say they plan to open-source code once the paper is accepted.
record.problems: Neuron-level evaluation covers 10 randomly selected neurons and uses ChatGPT-labeled top-activating sentences as ground truth. The paper notes that obtaining neuron ground truth is labor-intensive and says evaluating more neurons could benefit the process. It does not test descriptions against held-out firing examples.
record.rows_left_out: No other neuron-level results were omitted. Sentence-label precision/recall and inter-annotator agreement evaluate labeling sentences with descriptors, not neuron descriptions.

untested.parts: Shares of neuron poles with one, two or unexplained jobs in Qwen3-32B.
Shares across other models, dense and MoE, and across scale.
Re-reading canonical polysemantic neurons such as InceptionV1 cat/car; recursive generalization.
Effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the interpretable share.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict firing elsewhere.
Simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: Several features limit any wider reading. Only 10 neurons are evaluated. Ground truth comes from ChatGPT labels of the same top-activating sentences. Three broad descriptors, which fired for more than 80% of neurons, were discarded. Neurons can take multiple descriptors (C1 AND C2 ...), but the paper reports no share of monosemantic neurons. The paper does not test any version.

versions.untested_parts: The share of neuron poles with one, two, or not-yet-understood jobs, in Qwen3-32B or another model.
Shares across models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and recursive generalization.
The effects of architecture, regularization, and tool quality on interpretability shares, including estimates for vision models.
Whether attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model.
Whether descriptions based on activating examples fail to predict firing on examples not used to produce the descriptions.
Automated explanation scoring by simulating activations on new text.

rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation shown as shading in Figure 5; numeric value not stated.
rows.note: The evaluation uses the neurons' top activating sentences; it does not test whether the descriptions predict firing on new text.
rows.check: This is the study's own method evaluated against ChatGPT labels of top-activating sentences; it is not a measure of the claim. Linking to none is correct.
